support.quote: Plato relates that Socrates accounts for his seeming wiser than any other person because he does not imagine that he knows what he does not know.
I am better off than he is,—for he knows nothing, and thinks that he knows; I neither know nor think that I know.

assessments.note: Apology 21d (Jowett)

support.quote: The Pythia answered to Chaerephon that there was no man wiser.
he asked the oracle to tell him whether anyone was wiser than I was, and the Pythian prophetess answered, that there was no man wiser.

assessments.note: Apology 21a (Jowett)

support.quote: was held to determine the philosopher's guilt of two charges against the city of Athens: asebeia (impiety) and corruption of the youth.
It says that Socrates is a doer of evil, who corrupts the youth; and who does not believe in the gods of the state, but has other new divinities of his own. Such is the charge

assessments.note: Apology 24b (Jowett)

support.quote: Socrates’s irreverence, Meletus claimed, had resulted in the corruption of the city’s young men (Euthyphro 3c–d).
He died the next morning, in accordance with his sentence, after drinking hemlock.
The poisoner described the physical effects of the Conium maculatum variety of hemlock used for citizen executions (Bloch 2001), then Socrates cheerfully took the cup and drank.
You have only to walk about until your legs are heavy, and then to lie down, and the poison will act.
